content: This process must be informed by historical and current data on malaria transmission intensity and incidence, as well as contextual factors such as human host vulnerability, parasite and vector characteristics, past and present intervention coverage, acceptability, and equitable access to care. When the objective is malaria elimination, a similar process is required, though the interventions and cost-effectiveness analyses will differ from those used in high-burden settings. Despite significant reductions in malaria burden between 2000 and 2015, progress stalled by 2017, leaving the world off track to meet malaria morbidity and mortality reduction targets. In response, the High Burden to High Impact (HBHI) initiative was launched in 2018 to refocus efforts. This initiative emphasizes political commitment to reducing malaria, strategic use of data to drive impact, improved policies and strategies, and better coordination of national malaria responses. These activities are relevant not only for achieving the Global Technical Strategy (GTS) targets but also for ensuring continued progress toward malaria elimination in all endemic countries. The consolidated WHO Guidelines for malaria aim to provide the latest evidence-based recommendations to support countries in reducing and ultimately eliminating malaria. The guidelines focus on: 1. Offering evidence-based, context-sensitive recommendations for malaria prevention (e.g., vector control, chemoprevention, and vaccines), case management (diagnosis and treatment), and interventions for elimination and prevention of re-establishment. 2. Supporting WHO Member States in developing evidence-based national malaria policies tailored to all transmission settings. 3. Encouraging the use of local data for subnational stratification to optimize resource allocation and intervention impact. 4. Informing research agendas by identifying evidence gaps that constrain guidance development or weaken current recommendations. The guidelines are based on a synthesis of available evidence on the health effects of interventions, graded for certainty using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. This evidence is used to develop an evidence-to-decision (EtD) framework for each recommendation. Expert input is critical, particularly in areas where evidence is weak or absent. For example, vector control recommendations are informed by randomized controlled trials (RCTs), other studies, and the technical expertise of guideline development groups. The primary audience for these guidelines includes policymakers in ministries of health and managers of national malaria programs (NMPs) in endemic countries. They are also relevant to healthcare practitioners, environmental health professionals, procurement agencies, the private sector, civil society groups, international development partners, donors, and researchers. The guidelines emphasize equity, gender, and human rights, recognizing that health inequities, gender-based discrimination, and social determinants of health deprive many people of their right to health. Addressing these inequities is essential for achieving global and national malaria goals. Malaria is a life-threatening disease caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium, transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. The most common species infecting humans are P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale, with P. falciparum being the most dangerous. A fifth species, P. knowlesi, primarily infects non-human primates but is increasingly reported in humans in forested regions of Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific. Malaria transmission intensity depends on factors related to the parasite, vector, human host, and environment. Transmission is more intense in areas where mosquito lifespans are longer and where mosquitoes prefer feeding on humans. Female mosquito longevity is critical for malaria transmission, as the parasite requires 7–10 days to develop into an infectious form within the mosquito. Environmental factors such as temperature and humidity also influence mosquito survival. In Africa, where approximately 90% of global malaria cases occur, the strong human-biting preference of African vector species contributes to high transmission. Transmission intensity is typically assessed through the incidence of cases or the prevalence of infection. High-transmission areas are characterized by an annual parasite incidence of 450 or more cases per 1,000 population and a P. falciparum prevalence rate of ≥35%. Moderate-transmission areas have an incidence of 250–450 cases per 1,000 and a prevalence of 10–35%. Low-transmission areas have an incidence of 100–250 cases per 1,000 and a prevalence of 1–10%. Very low-transmission areas have an incidence of <100 cases per 1,000 and a prevalence of >0 but <1%. The clinical manifestations of malaria depend on the level of acquired immunity, which is influenced by the intensity and pattern of transmission in the area of residence. In high-transmission areas, partial immunity develops in early childhood, reducing the risk of severe malaria in older children and adults. In low-transmission areas, immunity develops more slowly, and both children and adults are at risk of severe malaria if untreated. Epidemics can occur in low-transmission areas when vectorial capacity increases suddenly, overwhelming health services. Effective malaria control requires evidence-informed recommendations and the strategic use of local data to tailor interventions to specific settings. Stratification of malaria risk at subnational levels is essential for identifying optimal intervention packages and prioritizing resource allocation. As countries progress toward elimination, finer-scale mapping and stratification are needed to target interventions effectively. The WHO guidelines emphasize a shift toward a problem-solving approach that uses local data to identify context-specific recommendations and intervention packages. This approach moves away from overly prescriptive recommendations and focuses on maximizing impact through tailored strategies. Accurate stratification of malaria transmission intensity is critical for effective targeting of interventions, particularly as countries approach elimination. In conclusion, these guidelines provide a framework for national malaria programs and their partners to adopt and adapt recommendations based on local contexts. High-quality surveillance data are essential for informing and evaluating program decisions, ensuring continued progress toward malaria elimination.
